strengths: Addresses a well-motivated problem: augmenting classical MWPM decoding with learned, syndrome-aware edge weights while retaining the algorithmic guarantees of the classical matcher, rather than replacing it outright.

Proposes a concrete solution to the non-differentiability of MWPM via a proxy edge-classification loss (BCE + entropy regularization), which is a reasonable and clearly described engineering contribution.

The hybrid GNN (TransformerConv) + Transformer-encoder architecture is described in substantial mathematical detail, including node/edge feature construction, gating mechanisms, and syndrome modulation, aiding reproducibility of the architecture itself.

Evaluation spans two code families (Toric and Rotated Surface codes) and two noise models (independent and depolarizing), with comparisons against MWPM, BPOSD-2, and a recent Transformer-based baseline (QECCT).

Reports threshold estimates that approach theoretical maximum-likelihood bounds and highlights a favorable parameter-count profile relative to QECCT (roughly constant ~3.9M parameters vs. QECCT's growth to 6.71M at L=10).
weaknesses: No decoding runtime/latency measurements are reported despite the introduction motivating the work partly around real-time decoding needs and despite the paper's own complexity analysis showing an O(E^2 d_hidden) term from the dense Transformer over all edges of a complete graph—this is a critical omission given real-time QEC decoding budgets are on the order of microseconds, and the paper does not address whether NMWPM is practically deployable.

LER curves (Figures 2-4) show no error bars or confidence intervals from finite-shot Monte Carlo sampling, a standard practice in this literature; several claimed improvements (e.g., threshold gains of 0.1-0.2 percentage points over QECCT, or 'modest' gains at L=6,8) are within a range where statistical significance cannot be assessed from the manuscript as presented.

No ablation studies isolate the contribution of individual architectural components (GNN-only vs. Transformer-only vs. combined), the entropy regularization term, or the choice of ground-truth generation heuristic, making it difficult to attribute performance gains to specific design choices versus generic capacity/overfitting to the training distribution.

The heuristic ground-truth generation procedure (clustering, localized MWPM, iterative permutation search, brute-force fallback) is complex and potentially introduces its own approximation bias into the supervised labels, but no analysis is given of how often the heuristic/brute-force fallback is triggered, how accurate the resulting labels are, or how sensitive results are to this procedure.

Tested code distances are modest (L up to 10 for Toric, L up to 7 for Rotated Surface code), and the claimed 'widening gap' advantage at larger L is extrapolated from very few data points; no evidence is given for scaling behavior at distances relevant to practical fault-tolerant hardware (L≈21+).

The experiments appear restricted to code-capacity noise models (no circuit-level/measurement noise), which limits the practical significance of the claimed advances for realistic fault-tolerant QEC pipelines where syndrome extraction is itself noisy.

No statement of code, data, or trained-model release is provided, and several practical details (training set size per code/distance, time to generate ground-truth labels, exact QECCT retraining/hyperparameter protocol referenced only as 'with our implementation') are omitted, limiting reproducibility.

The comparison methodology for baselines (e.g., whether QECCT was retrained under identical conditions, with matched training budgets) is not fully specified, raising concerns about the fairness of the reported comparisons.

strengths: The paper proposes a reasonably well-engineered hybrid architecture (GNN + Transformer) that augments rather than replaces MWPM, preserving the perfect-matching guarantee of the classical algorithm while injecting learned, syndrome-conditioned edge weights.

The method/background sections are thorough and the architecture (node/edge feature construction, TransformerConv backbone, global Transformer encoder, NLL weight conversion) is described in substantial, mostly reproducible detail, including diagrams (Fig. 1, Fig. 7) and an explicit algorithmic ground-truth-generation procedure (Algorithm 2).

Evaluation spans two code families (Toric and Rotated Surface) under two noise models (independent and depolarizing) and reports threshold estimates that approach the theoretical maximum-likelihood bound, with comparisons to MWPM, BPOSD-2, and a Transformer baseline (QECCT).
The reported parameter count of NMWPM is nearly constant across code distances, contrasting favorably with the baseline QECCT model whose parameter count grows substantially with code size.
weaknesses: All experiments use code-capacity (single-round, 2D) noise models rather than the circuit-level noise with repeated, faulty syndrome extraction that is the practically relevant setting for real QEC hardware and the standard benchmark in the decoder literature; this severely limits the significance of the claimed gains, since code-capacity thresholds (e.g., 10.3%/11%) bear little resemblance to realistic circuit-level thresholds (~0.5-1%).

No error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests are reported for any LER curve or threshold estimate (Figs. 2-4), making it impossible to judge whether the reported improvements (e.g., 17.9% vs 17.8% QECCT threshold, or 10.95% vs 10.8%/10.7%) are statistically meaningful rather than noise from finite Monte Carlo sampling.

The Transformer encoder operates over all edges of a fully connected defect graph, yielding a stated O(E^2 d_hidden) complexity; since E scales polynomially with the (already small) lattice sizes tested (L up to 10), this raises serious scalability concerns that directly undercut the paper's framing around 'real-time decoding' and 'scalability,' yet no wall-clock inference latency or throughput is reported anywhere in the paper to substantiate practical viability versus MWPM/BPOSD-2/QECCT.

No ablation studies are provided to justify the many architectural design choices (GNN vs. Transformer contributions, modulated syndrome encoding, entropy regularization term, learned embedding table, specific node/edge features), so it is unclear which components drive the reported gains or whether simpler alternatives would perform comparably.

Only very small code distances are evaluated (Toric L∈{6,8,10}, Rotated Surface L∈{5,7}), and for the more practically relevant Rotated Surface code the model only achieves 'parity' with QECCT at the largest tested distance (L=7), suggesting the advantage may not persist or may even reverse at larger, more realistic distances—yet no larger-L results or discussion of this trend's extrapolation is given.

The supervised ground-truth generation relies on a heuristic clustering + local MWPM + permutation-search procedure whose fidelity to the true maximum-likelihood error chain is not validated or quantified (e.g., via comparison to brute-force or known-optimal labels at small L), so the quality/bias of the training signal itself is unverified and could confound the reported performance gains.

Reproducibility is only partially supported: no code or trained models are stated to be released, and dataset generation / exact baseline reimplementation details (e.g., for QECCT, which the authors note they re-implemented) are not fully specified, making independent verification difficult.

Minor presentation issues (e.g., 'NNWPM' vs 'NMWPM' inconsistency in Figure 3) and the framing of 'advantage' in several places is not consistently supported by the magnitude of the reported differences once lack of statistical testing is considered.

strengths: The proposed hybrid architecture (GNN for local syndrome topology + Transformer for global dependencies, feeding dynamic edge weights into classical MWPM) is a reasonable and well-motivated design that preserves the algorithmic guarantees of MWPM while injecting learned, syndrome-conditioned priors.
The paper provides a thorough and clearly written background on stabilizer codes, degeneracy, and the MWPM/Blossom formalism, making the technical setting accessible.

The proxy loss (BCE + entropy regularization) is a sensible way to approximate gradient signal through the otherwise non-differentiable MWPM step, and the paper gives intuition for why confident, polarized edge probabilities are beneficial for the downstream minimization.

Evaluation spans two code families (Toric and Rotated Surface) and two noise models (independent and depolarizing), and compares against multiple baselines (MWPM, BPOSD-2, QECCT), with reported threshold values approaching the maximum-likelihood bound.
The model analysis section (weight distribution dynamics) offers some qualitative insight into training behavior and provides at least partial interpretability of the learned weights.
Reported parameter efficiency (near-constant ~3.9M parameters vs. QECCT's growth to 6.71M) is a potentially meaningful practical advantage if verified rigorously.
weaknesses: No error bars, confidence intervals, or reported shot counts are given for any LER curve or threshold estimate, despite LER curves being inherently noisy, especially near threshold and at low physical error rates; without this, claimed improvements (e.g., 17-50% LER reduction, threshold differences of a few tenths of a percent) cannot be judged as statistically significant.

Only very small code distances are tested (L=6,8,10 for the Toric code and L=5,7 for the Rotated Surface code). Given that the Transformer component has quadratic complexity in the number of edges (as the paper itself notes, O(E^2 d_hidden)), the lack of any experiments at larger, more practically relevant distances is a significant gap for a method whose central claim is about handling 'long-range global dependencies' that matter more at scale.

No wall-clock runtime or throughput comparison is provided against MWPM/PyMatching or QECCT, despite decoding speed being a first-order practical concern for real-time QEC decoders; only a theoretical big-O complexity argument is given, which is insufficient to support claims about practical viability.

The ground-truth label generation procedure (Algorithm 2) is a multi-stage heuristic (clustering, local MWPM with Manhattan weights, iterative permutation, timed brute-force fallback) that is not fully specified (e.g., stopping/permutation criteria, frequency of fallback invocation, computational cost of generating training data) and raises concerns about label quality/bias as well as reproducibility.

It is unclear whether the QECCT and BPOSD-2 baselines were reimplemented by the authors or taken from original sources/other codebases; the paper notes 'our implementation' inconsistently, raising concerns about fair, like-for-like comparison (e.g., matched training budget, matched definition of LER, matched noise sampling).

No ablations isolate the contribution of individual architectural components (GNN alone vs. Transformer alone vs. combined, entropy regularization on/off, node feature choices such as positional encodings or learned embeddings), making it hard to attribute the reported gains to specific design choices versus simply more parameters/training.

No code or data release is mentioned, and the architecture has many bespoke feature-engineering choices (multiple MLP projections, distance embeddings, modulated syndrome, positional encodings) that would be difficult to reproduce exactly from the text alone.

The experiments use code-capacity-like noise models (independent and depolarizing) rather than circuit-level noise with measurement errors, which is the setting of greatest practical relevance for fault-tolerant QEC; this limits the significance of the claimed advances for real decoders.

The comparison to prior ML-based decoders (e.g., GNN-based decoder of Lange et al. 2025, cited in related work) is absent from the experimental section, leaving a gap relative to the most relevant class of competing methods beyond QECCT.

strengths: The paper proposes a well-motivated hybrid architecture (GNN + Transformer) that augments rather than replaces the classical MWPM decoder, retaining the polynomial-time algorithmic guarantees of Blossom while injecting learned, syndrome-conditioned edge weights.

The reported results are strong and close to known maximum-likelihood bounds for the toric code (17.9% vs 18.9% depolarizing, 10.95% vs 11.0% independent), and the method is shown to outperform strong ML baselines (QECCT, BPOSD-2) as well as classical MWPM/MWPM-Corr across multiple code families (toric, rotated surface, repetition) and noise models (independent, depolarizing, circuit-level).

Broad experimental scope: ablations (geometric/edge features, entropy term, MIN vs MAX aggregation, MLP vs Transformer backbone), parameter-count and inference-time comparisons against QECCT, and generalization studies (interpolation, extrapolation to unseen error rates, and transfer learning across code distances) that go beyond a single headline metric.

The paper is clearly written with a thorough background section, explicit algorithmic pseudocode for both inference (Algorithm 1) and ground-truth construction (Algorithm 2), and detailed appendices covering boundary handling, training hyperparameters, and dataset-generation timeout protocols, which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: The proxy training objective (BCE + entropy regularization on edge probabilities) is only loosely connected to the actual MWPM objective it is meant to approximate; there is no theoretical argument or empirical evidence that minimizing this edge-classification loss is aligned with minimizing the downstream logical error rate beyond the reported empirical outcome, leaving the central 'differentiable training objective' contribution somewhat heuristic.

Ground-truth label generation relies on a heuristic clustering + localized MWPM procedure that picks 'the first valid matching it encounters' among many degenerate equivalence-class representatives; this arbitrary tie-breaking could bias the learned edge probabilities in ways not analyzed, and the impact of this choice on final decoder performance is not ablated.

Scalability evidence is limited: the largest toric code tested is L=12 and rotated surface code L=9, while the paper itself acknowledges quadratic edge-count scaling of the Transformer encoder; no experiments probe whether NMWPM remains tractable or competitive at the larger code distances (L=20+) relevant to fault-tolerant hardware roadmaps.

Circuit-level noise evaluation (arguably the most practically relevant setting) is confined to very small repetition codes (L=3,5) and a single small rotated surface code instance (L=3, 3 rounds), which is insufficient to support claims of practical readiness under realistic noise.

No statistical uncertainty (error bars, confidence intervals, number of trials/shots) is reported for any LER or threshold estimate, making it difficult to assess whether the reported improvements over QECCT/BPOSD-2/MWPM are statistically robust, particularly given some differences appear marginal (e.g., rotated code QECCT 17.2% vs NMWPM 17.7%).

The comparative threshold table (Table 5) aggregates numbers from disparate papers using different codes, noise models, and definitions of threshold, which weakens the validity of directly ranking NMWPM against them.

A references entry ('Peled, Y., Zenati, D., and Nachmani, E. NMWPM source code. [Repository], 2026') explicitly names the authors, which appears to break double-blind anonymity for the ICML review process.

strengths: The hybrid GNN+Transformer architecture for predicting dynamic MWPM edge weights is a reasonable and moderately novel engineering design, and the paper provides substantial architectural detail (node/edge featurization, modulated syndrome encoding, gating mechanism) that aids reproducibility of the model itself.

The experimental scope is broad: toric and rotated surface codes, independent and depolarizing noise, circuit-level noise via Stim, repetition codes, plus ablations, parameter-efficiency comparisons, inference-time benchmarking, and transfer-learning/extrapolation studies.
Comparison against multiple baselines (MWPM, BPOSD-2, MWPM-Corr, QECCT) and a literature table of reported thresholds situates the method within the existing landscape.

The paper explicitly discusses boundary handling (virtual nodes for rotated codes) and ground-truth generation challenges arising from code degeneracy, showing awareness of important implementation subtleties.
weaknesses: The central claim of a 'differentiable proxy loss' that enables 'end-to-end optimization' through the non-differentiable MWPM algorithm is misleading: the actual training objective (BCE + entropy on edge probabilities) never backpropagates through the MWPM step at all. The network is trained as an independent supervised edge-classification task against heuristically generated labels, and MWPM is only invoked at inference. This is not an end-to-end differentiable-MWPM training scheme as advertised, but a decoupled two-stage pipeline, which the framing in the abstract/intro overstates.

Ground-truth label generation is heuristic and admittedly arbitrary: the clustering/local-MWPM procedure 'assigns the first valid matching it encounters' among many logically-equivalent options, with no justification that this choice yields labels that are optimal or even consistent across samples. This raises concerns about bias/noise in supervision and casts doubt on how the trained model can approach near-maximum-likelihood thresholds.

Threshold estimates (e.g., 17.9% vs. 18.9% ML bound) are reported without any visible crossing-point/finite-size-scaling methodology, error bars, confidence intervals, or repeated-trial variance. Given these values are derived from a narrow range of code distances (L up to 10-12), the precision implied by numbers like '17.9%' is not substantiated by the presented analysis.

Scalability is questionable: the Transformer encoder operates over a fully connected graph of defects with O(E^2) attention complexity, and the paper explicitly notes QECCT runs out of memory at L=12, yet does not clearly demonstrate NMWPM's own behavior at higher defect densities/larger lattices beyond modest sizes, leaving real-world scalability to practical code distances (L>20, as used in industry roadmaps) unaddressed.

The reference list contains what appear to be self-citations exposing author identity (e.g., 'Peled, Y., Zenati, D., and Nachmani, E. NMWPM source code. [Repository], 2026' and other Zenati/Nachmani entries), which is a serious concern for a purportedly blind review process and raises procedural/ethical questions that should be resolved before acceptance.
Several numeric inconsistencies appear in the text (e.g., QECCT described as reaching '6.71M parameters' in prose but '6.64M' in Table 1), suggesting insufficient care in result reporting.

The significance of the proposed method is somewhat incremental relative to existing neural-augmented decoders (QECCT, GNN-based decoders, transformer decoders cited in Related Work); the reported gains over QECCT are described as 'modest' at smaller lattice sizes, and the paper does not clearly isolate which architectural component (GNN vs Transformer vs ground-truth heuristic) is responsible for the claimed near-ML-bound performance beyond a basic ablation.

Circuit-level noise evaluation (repetition code, rotated X memory) is limited to very small code distances (L=3,5) and short few-round experiments, providing weak evidence that gains persist under realistic, larger-scale circuit noise relevant to practical QEC.

strengths: The paper presents a well-motivated hybrid architecture (GNN + Transformer) that augments rather than replaces the classical MWPM decoder, preserving its algorithmic guarantees while injecting learned, syndrome-conditioned edge weights.

Extensive empirical validation across multiple code families (toric, rotated surface, repetition) and noise models (independent, depolarizing, circuit-level), with thresholds approaching the theoretical maximum-likelihood bounds (17.9%/18.9% and 10.95%/11.0%).
Thorough ablation study (geometric features, edge features, entropy term, aggregation strategy, MLP vs. Transformer) that isolates the contribution of individual architectural components.
Favorable parameter efficiency and inference-time comparisons against the QECCT transformer baseline, showing near-constant parameter count and better scaling with code distance.

Additional analyses of generalization, interpolation/extrapolation to noise rates outside the training range, and transfer learning across code distances, which strengthen claims about learned representations being non-trivial and reusable.
Reasonably detailed reproducibility information in the appendices (hyperparameters, timeout/filtering protocol for ground-truth generation, boundary handling for rotated codes).
weaknesses: The central claim of solving MWPM's non-differentiability via a 'novel proxy loss' is overstated: the method does not backpropagate through the matching algorithm at all; it trains a supervised edge-classification network independently and only uses MWPM at inference. This reframing should be stated more precisely, and the technique (BCE edge classification feeding into classical matching) closely resembles prior GNN/Transformer decoder works (e.g., Lange et al. 2025, Bausch et al. 2024, Choukroun & Wolf 2024) cited in the related work, somewhat limiting the claimed novelty.

The ground-truth generation procedure relies on a heuristic clustering + local MWPM + brute-force fallback with early-stopping on the first valid matching found; given topological code degeneracy, this introduces a potentially biased/inconsistent training signal that is not rigorously justified as representative of the true posterior over error chains.

Baseline thresholds are sourced inconsistently from different papers/implementations (e.g., MWPM at 16.0% from Wang et al. 2010, BPOSD numbers described as 'based on our experiments'), which makes head-to-head comparisons less reliable; no confidence intervals or finite-size-scaling fit details are given for the reported thresholds.

The Transformer encoder's self-attention over all edges in the fully connected defect graph incurs O(E^2) complexity, which the authors acknowledge, yet empirical scaling is only shown up to L=10-12; it is unclear how the approach behaves at the larger code distances relevant to fault-tolerant thresholds.

No statistical reporting (confidence intervals, number of Monte Carlo shots) accompanies the LER/threshold curves, making it hard to assess the significance of reported improvements, especially the narrow margins over QECCT in several settings.

Reproducibility beyond the text is unclear: the citation to source code ('NMWPM source code, [Repository], 2026') appears to be a self-reference without a confirmed public link in the manuscript, leaving full reproducibility unverified.

The entropy regularization is formulated in an unconventional way ('BCE of the probability vector with itself') without clear mathematical justification or comparison to standard entropy minimization formulations, and its benefit in the ablation is only 'slight'.
